questions.title: A critical service becomes unavailable during peak traffic. How do you handle the incident?
questions.quick: I declare an incident, assign roles, and focus first on restoring service. I check the golden signals, recent changes, and the saturated resource, then mitigate with rollback, scaling, load shedding, feature flags or a static fallback page. I communicate status regularly. Afterwards I run a blameless review and fix capacity, autoscaling, backpressure, and dependency isolation so peaks degrade gracefully.
questions.revision: Declare incident, restore service via rollback, scaling or shedding, communicate, then review and build graceful degradation.
questions.detailed:
During an outage, restore service and communicate before seeking the root cause.

{{diagram:outage}}

## Clarify

What is the user impact and since when? Which services are affected? Who is the incident commander, and who communicates? What is the severity and the target recovery?

## Observe

Read the golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Check load balancer health, autoscaling activity, CPU, memory, connection counts, queue depth and dependency health. Check change history and the status of cloud providers.

## Isolate

Find the saturated or failing component and the failure sequence: did one dependency fail and cascade through retries? Check whether autoscaling was too slow, limits were hit, or health checks were removing healthy nodes.

## Diagnose

Look for retry storms, a thundering herd after a cache expiry, exhausted connection pools, scale-up limits, a cold-start delay, or database saturation. Confirm with traces and metrics timelines.

| Signal | Likely cause | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dependency failure cascading | Retries and no isolation | Circuit breaker, bulkheads |
| Autoscaling too slow | Reactive scaling lag | Pre-scale, scheduled scaling |
| Database saturated | Capacity or heavy queries | Shed load, cache, scale reads |

Illustrative snippet (adapt to your stack):

```
# Illustrative Logs Insights query: errors by minute
fields @timestamp, status
| filter status >= 500
| stats count() by bin(1m)
```

## Mitigate

Roll back suspect changes, scale out manually with raised limits, enable load shedding for non-critical traffic, turn off expensive features, serve cached or static content, add a waiting room if needed. Update status every <interval>.

## Recover

Restore capacity gradually, watch for secondary failures as traffic returns, and confirm normal service. Send a final customer update.

## Prevent

Run a blameless review with a timeline. Add load tests at expected peak plus margin, warm capacity before known events, circuit breakers, bulkheads, backpressure, graceful degradation and runbooks, and test failover regularly.

## Common mistakes

- Debugging for the root cause before restoring service.
- Poor communication, so teams duplicate effort.
- Autoscaling that reacts only after saturation.

diagrams.alt: Peak traffic reaches a load balancer and service. When saturation is detected the incident commander declares an incident. Mitigations include rollback, scaling, load shedding and static fallback, while communication updates run in parallel and a review follows recovery.

questions.title: A production issue cannot be reproduced locally. How do you approach it?
questions.quick: I stop trying to guess and extract more evidence from production: correlation IDs, structured logs, traces, and request samples, with sensitive data protected. I identify what differs in production: data, scale, concurrency, config, versions, network and timing. Then I recreate those conditions in staging or a production-like replica, add targeted logging behind a flag, and test hypotheses with canaries. I finish by improving observability.
questions.revision: Collect evidence via logs and traces, list production differences, recreate them safely, test hypotheses with flags and canaries.
questions.detailed:
If you cannot reproduce it, find out what production has that your machine lacks.

{{diagram:repro}}

## Clarify

What exactly is the symptom, how often, and for whom? Is it tied to specific users, data, regions, browsers or times? How severe is the impact, and is there a workaround?

## Observe

Gather correlation IDs from affected requests, structured logs, traces, error reports and, for frontend issues, session replay with privacy controls. Compare affected and unaffected requests using a Logs Insights or equivalent query.

## Isolate

Find the common factor in failures: tenant, data shape, version, instance, region, device, or time window. Compare configuration and dependency versions between environments. Look for race conditions that need concurrency.

## Diagnose

Typical differences: data volume and unusual records, feature flags and config, environment variables, time zones, concurrency, caches, network latency, third-party behaviour and browser extensions. Rank hypotheses and design one cheap test for each.

| Signal | Likely cause | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fails for one tenant or record | Data-specific | Sanitised copy of the data |
| Intermittent under concurrency | Race or contention | Load test, add locking or idempotency |
| Only some devices or browsers | Client environment | Session replay, device matrix |

Illustrative snippet (adapt to your stack):

```
# Illustrative: compare failing and passing requests
fields @timestamp, requestId, tenantId, version, @message
| filter @message like /<error pattern>/
| stats count() by tenantId, version
```

## Mitigate

If users are harmed, use a flag to disable the feature or apply a workaround. Add temporary, scoped debug logging or sampling behind a flag, and avoid logging secrets or personal data.

## Recover

Reproduce with a sanitised production data copy, replayed traffic or a load test with concurrency. Confirm the fix on a canary, and keep the added telemetry if useful.

## Prevent

Improve observability with correlation IDs, richer traces, error context, feature flag visibility and data-quality checks. Record the finding in a runbook.

## Common mistakes

- Guessing and changing code with no evidence.
- Logging sensitive data while debugging.
- Never keeping the extra telemetry or learning.

diagrams.title: Reproducing a production-only issue
diagrams.alt: Evidence from logs, traces and correlation IDs is collected and used to find the factor common to failing requests. Differences between production and local are listed as hypotheses, tested in a production-like environment or canary, and the learning feeds better observability.
